title: Griha pravesha: the hall opens
hookLine: Maya goes north for his materials, comes back with a mace and a conch, and builds a hall with a pool that looks like floor
carry: griha pravesha: a new home opens by feeding people

cards: Before Maya lays a single stone, he leaves. He goes north, past Kailasa, the text says, to a lake called Bindu, where he'd stored treasures long before.

He comes back carrying gifts: a heavy mace bound in gold for Bhima, a conch called Devadatta, with a sound that carries, for Arjuna, and crystal and jewels and everything a hall like no other would need.
Only then does he start building.

teach.b: The text spends a long time on this hall.

teach.h: A POOL THAT LOOKS LIKE FLOOR.
teach.b: Walls that shine like the sun. Trees in bloom inside, and a cool breeze. In the middle, a pool: lotuses on the water, crystal steps going down.
The water was so still and clear that kings who came to see it, the text says, took it for solid floor, and fell in. Hold onto that pool; this serial will come back to it.
Now watch what Yudhishthira does before he steps inside. He feeds a great crowd of brahmanas: rice and ghee, honey, fruit. He gives away cows.
There's music, there are offerings, and only after all that does he enter. Hindu families still open a home this way.
It's called griha pravesha, entering the house. You don't just carry in the boxes.

There's a puja, often to Ganesha first; many families boil milk until it spills over, a sign of plenty; and there's food, lots of it, for the priest, the relatives, the neighbors, before anyone sleeps there.
Behind it is anna dana, the gift of food, which Hindus often call one of the greatest gifts there is.

teach.h: A HOME BEGINS WHERE PEOPLE WERE FED.
teach.b: A home, or a king's hall, begins as a place where people were fed. Then the hall fills. Sages come, kings come, singers come.
That's the other half of the word sabha: the gathering. A sabha with no one in it is only a building.

how: Moving into a new home, Hindu families often hold a griha pravesha, a house-entering ceremony: a puja, often to Ganesha first, milk boiled until it overflows in many families, and a meal shared with guests before the family settles in.

o: a hall, and the gathering of people who meet there
the treasure Maya kept at Lake Bindu
a palace pool built to look like solid floor

games.q: the builder's gifts — tap the pairs.
p: goes north to Lake Bindu first
a heavy mace bound in gold

s: Maya built the hall only from what was on hand at Indraprastha
he went north past Kailasa to Lake Bindu first, the text says, and brought back materials and gifts.
visiting kings fell into the hall's pool
the water was so clear they took it for solid floor.
Yudhishthira entered the hall the moment it was done
he fed a great crowd of brahmanas and gave gifts first.

games.q: you're Yudhishthira. the hall Maya built is finished and waiting for you. what do you do first?
o: walk in quietly and see it alone.
feed a great crowd and give gifts, then enter.
invite rival kings to come and admire it.
games.why: he feeds brahmanas, gives away cows, has music and offerings, and only then walks in. the hall opens with feeding, not with showing off.

practice: Next time you eat today, do what many Hindus do before the first bite: offer it first, a moment of thanks, or a little set aside for God. If you don't pray, let the pause be your thanks.
Then bring to mind one person you could feed this week, a guest, a neighbor, a friend who's had a long day, and picture setting the plate in front of them.

wordCard.voice: Sabha. A hall, and the assembly that meets in it. Maya's hall at Indraprastha, opened the way Hindu homes still open: by feeding people first.

orig.note: Sanskrit sabhā: a hall, and the assembly that gathers in it.

carryVoice: Your line: griha pravesha: a new home opens by feeding people. The people make it a sabha. Day seven hundred forty-seven, done.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Sabhakriya Parva (Maya fetches materials from Lake Bindu; the mace and the conch Devadatta; the hall and its pool; Yudhishthira's entry)
